keyVerseText: And the king of Israel said unto Jehoshaphat, There is yet one man, Micaiah the son of Imlah, by whom we may enquire of the LORD: but I hate him; for he doth not prophesy good concerning me, but evil. And Jehoshaphat said, Let not the king say so.
rootMeaning: The root of יִמְלָא (Yimlâʼ) is מָלֵא (mâlêʼ), which means 'to fill' or 'to be full.' This root conveys a sense of completeness, fulfillment, and abundance. The name יִמְלָא literally means 'whom God will fill up,' suggesting a person filled or endowed by God, which adds a deeper spiritual dimension beyond a mere proper name.
usageInScripture: The word יִמְלָא occurs four times in Scripture, consistently as a proper name referring to an Israelite, specifically the father of the prophet Micaiah. The top translations show it rendered as 'of Imlah' or 'of Imla,' indicating a stable personal name rather than a common noun. This usage highlights the name's function as an identifier linked to prophetic authority.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding יִמְלָא as 'whom God will fill up' enriches our grasp of biblical identity, emphasizing that God equips and fills His servants for His purposes. The connection to Micaiah, a prophet who faithfully delivers God's word—even when unwelcome—reminds believers that divine filling empowers truth-telling and faithful witness. This reflects the broader biblical theme that God fills His people with His Spirit to accomplish His will, underscoring reliance on divine provision rather than human strength.
keyVerseReflection: In 1 Kings 22:8, the phrase 'Micaiah the son of Imlah' identifies the prophet by his father’s name, יִמְלָא, linking Micaiah to a lineage 'filled by God.' The verse highlights Micaiah as the one through whom the king may inquire of the LORD, despite the king's dislike for his unfavorable prophecies. This personal name thus anchors the prophet’s divine authority and the sober truth he brings, reminding readers that God’s filling equips His messengers even in challenging circumstances.
